title: 90+ days, 3,240 commits, 1,000,000+ lines of C#: a system-by-system breakdown of my AI-built voxel RPG (with numbers).
author: block-boi-dior
selftext:
I've been building (this project which I will not name here), a voxel open-world RPG for my son and I to play together, with Claude Code since late August. I've been lurking on this sub for months eagerly waiting to share what I have made. What started as making a game for my 7 year old son and I to play, turned into a mission to match triple AAA level quality using just AI. No slop, and to prove to AI haters that time, effort and love is very much still needed to make AI games.

I am aware of the anti-AI crowd that lurks on this sub and so I am intentionally leaving out as much identifying info as possible. 

Here's the project so far:

**TLDR stats**

* Development time - 90+ days 
* Commits - 3,240 (\~40 a day) 
* C# \~1,000,000+ lines across 2,000+ files 
* Stack - .NET 10, [Silk.NET](http://Silk.NET) (OpenGL/windowing/input), NAudio, LiteNetLib (UDP), Concentus (Opus), SQLite (server) 
* No engine. No Unity, no Unreal, no Godot. Everything below is our own code on top of raw OpenGL.

\---

1. Rendering

**Voxels** \- 2 voxels per metre (50 cm blocks), 32-voxel chunks.

**View distance** \- full-detail chunks out to 16 chunks (256 m), then LOD "far country" tiles out to 384 chunks (6 km). Getting the view distance this high while remaining optimized was quite a big lift. It took roughly two weeks (with breaks) for Opus to write this feature.

**Atomosphere** \- 4x MSAA, 2048 px shadow maps, volumetric fog, depth of field, per-biome atmosphere (each biome sets its own haze, light and fog), and a distance-haze model tuned so the near half of the view stays clear.

**DLSS Integration** \- NVIDIA provides it's DLSS code free and openly on github. DLSS through Streamline, and HDR-safe borderless fullscreen.



2. World generation

**Five rings** at 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 km radius. Each ring is a difficulty tier, and the world gets stranger as you go out. The starting ring is peaceful and cozy biomes which gradually become more hostile as you explore outward

**28 biomes**, from forests and beaches to the Glasswaste and the Wicked Plains.

**The Farlands** the outer ring is floating islands and sky villages hanging over a void. This is the endgame area where you'll need a flying mount to traverse it. This area also holds some of the best gear in the game.

**Villages** are sited on 512 m planning cells. There are 12 village layouts, plus a neighbour rule so two villages joined by a road never wear the same layout. Every village is missing at least one or more special benches / NPCs with the idea of encouraging exploration and "finding a village with a bench you need."

**Rivers, roads** between villages, and roughly 20 POIs so far (camps, ruins, giant tree, giant tower), and 5 dungeons (so far) built from 73 hand-made rooms.

**Content** 202 structures and 189 building designs. Every building is authored in an in-game editor that let's me build new buildings when I need them and them to the generated world.



3. Combat

**Weapons** 11 archetypes, including swords, greatblades, glaives, spears (throwable), bows, muskets, rifles and pistols (with reloads), shields, and dual wield. This was a huge chunk of developement. It spanned several weeks and a ton of my testing and tweaking time went here

**Abilities** 14 (Leap, Fissure, Whirlwind, Charge, Venom Spit, Burrow and more), each with 5 tiers. Tier 5 is the biggest version of each move. Players learn these skills by killing the boss that uses it. Once learned, abilities can be upgrade at an alter with a relic (collectable).

**Relics** found in the world and offered at a church altar to raise an ability a tier.

**Creatures (still a lot of work here)** 95 designs (not all of them deslopped yet). Bosses include the Foreman (shown in trailer), the Core Serpent (a segmented body that rears to bite and lashes its tail and also in the trailer), the Bough King on top of a giant tree, and a world boss: the Hollow Tempest, fought from a gunship in the Farlands sky, then on its island (this is the final boss of the game and I love how this fight turned out).



4. Life and crafting

**Six life skills:** fishing, farming, cooking, harvesting, forging and smithing. Level up by doing them, not by assigning points.

215 items (handcrafted in-game items so far) and 416 prop items (chairs, benches, chests, etc).

**Benches** weapon forge (players can fully design every weapon type use a layered grid system I came up with), armour forge, carpenter, vehicle bench (player's can also build their own mounts (with some limitations), a smelting furnace (brass, steel), an oven (for cooking your food), and flax mills (processing flax into linen).

**Farming** A full indepth farming system with growing times and required tilled ground. Crops can be planted in public fields (like Archage) and are owned by whoever planted them; private plots exist too on player owned Homestead.



5. Towns and homesteads

**Towns** (villages) are a ket part of the game. They contain merchants, special creater NPC (16 NPC types), mayors who can be elected and can edit their village, a Block Bank, and town job boards.

**Homesteads** (a mid-late game reward) Player's can by Land deeds from the local mayor and claim land, then lay out roads, walls, fields and buildings inside their claimed plot. This works online as well.

Drafting table This is one of the special NPC types in towns but is a key feature to the homestead system. Player's can learn to draft construction plans which let's them draw their own house block by block and and then place it on their land. There are also 16 prefab plans you can buy from a drafter for 1,000–4,500 coins.

**Map & fog of war** 32 m squares with a 260 m sight radius, so the map fills in as you travel.



6. Vehicles

**Five kinds** so far - bicycle, motor car, hot-air balloon, biplane and sailing boat, with 8 designs between them. The vehicle bench lets you build your ownwith limitations like (must include four wheels that all touch the ground at the same Y point, and so on).

**Biplane** (one of my favorite features) a real (simple) flight model. Thrust, drag and gravity act on airspeed, so climbing costs speed and diving buys it back. It stalls at 13 m/s, takes off at 15, needs 17 to recover (that hysteresis stops it flickering in and out of a stall), and tops out at 38 m/s.

Boats: sail with the wind, heel, catch gusts, and leave wakes. You can also fish off of your boat. This is so players can deep sea fish and catch fun big fish like Octopus and Whales.



7. Audio

**One mixer for everything** 44.1 kHz float stereo, fed to the device in 4 × 20 ms blocks.

**Every sound lands on its exact sample**, at a fixed 83 ms latency. This came out of a real bug with the default 150 ms buffers, footsteps snapped to a 150 ms grid and drifted against the walk animation. I spent a lot of time deslopping the sound and I am still not happy with all noises.

**Limits** 24 voices and 6 sustained loops, a soft limiter on the master, per-biome nature soundscapes, 332 sound effects, and 16 music tracks driven by a music director (exploration, combat, boss). Suno was used to create the music based on my personal musical taste.

**Voice chat** proximity voice online, Opus at 48 kHz in 20 ms frames.



8. Online

**Authoritative dedicated server** 30 Hz tick, 20 Hz snapshots. Clients send 60 input frames a second, bundled at 30 Hz. I learned from New World that the server needs to tell the client what the player has and not the other way around :D

**Shared simulation** the server runs the same movement and combat code as the client. Other players' poses are computed server-side from that shared code, so nobody can be drawn somewhere their client merely claimed.

**Network LiteNetLib** over UDP, with SQLite for persistence.

**Features groups**, **online homesteads**, **mayors**, and the **world boss with allies.**

Bots headless bot clients that play the real protocol, for load testing.



9. Tooling (the part I'm proudest of)

**12 in-game editors ("forges")** weapons, armour, assets, biomes, buildings, dungeons, homes, creatures, POIs, quests, villages and vehicles. Content is made in the game, not in code. This is where AI haters wont care. Every item, POI, dungeon, building, town, mobs, NPC and more can be and are created in the "Gamemaker Portal" This was one of the first things I built. A toolset to allow me to build assets for the game.

**Official content library** a shared library that every machine syncs to, with revisions, so test builds pull the same content wherever they're built.



How it's actually built with AI

**I direct, design and playtest**; Claude Code writes nearly all the code. I describe what I want in plain language ("New feature request - Add farming to the game via fixed plots and grow cycles. We will have the following crops for growing....") and the work happens in Claude Code sessions running on my desktop and a home server, each on its own git branch.

**Tests are the guardrail,** not a nice-to-have. 42% of the codebase is self-tests. Some tests pin exact source lines, so one AI session can't quietly undo a rule another session put in. A full run takes about 2 hours, so day to day we run only the sections a change touches.

**Every feature carries its "why"**. Code comments quote the request that created the feature, with the date, so the next session knows what it's protecting. For example "The Gamemaker, 2026-11-07: "we need to record sound when using the built in game recording feature"\`.

**Hard rules live in a CLAUDE.md.** (Crtical!!) One example: a building in the world and its design in the editor must always match, so an editor save can never silently revert a scripted change.

**The biggest lesson: verify everything.** The first take with sound came out as white noise. Claude caught it by looking at the spectrogram, then traced it to an audio-library quirk (a byte buffer handed over as a float array). The fix shipped with a test that fails on the old code.

  
That's all I got for now and I am just getting started. My goal again is to build something polished with depth for my son and I to play and to show that AI can empower super ordinary people to finally launch their ideas. The difference between an AI slop game and one that isn't: is time, love and effort.

  
**You can download a demo** here if you're interested in playing [https://147.182.181.130/ky637kgajn/](https://147.182.181.130/ky637kgajn/)
